item.title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.
item.abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

item.title: Reshaping the scissors: From directed evolution to AI-driven design for enhanced Cas performance.
item.abstract: CRISPR/Cas gene editing holds great promise for applications in agricultural breeding and gene therapy; however, native Cas proteins face bottlenecks such as off-target effects, PAM limitations, and delivery challenges. This review explores a three-tiered, progressive, and synergistic analytical framework comprising directed evolution, rational structural design, and integrated protein engineering. Following the logic of "random exploration-precision modification-system integration," it systematically clarifies the principles, advantages, disadvantages, and complementary interactions among these three optimization techniques. By comprehensively mapping the entire technical pathway for Cas protein improvement, this study fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field and provides a theoretical framework for tiered, synergistic modification to support the development of high-performance editors. The paper further analyzes a novel research and development paradigm in which AI and protein language models profoundly empower Cas modification. It summarizes intelligent toolchains such as structure prediction, virtual mutation, and de novo design of artificial Cas proteins, and highlights the unique advantages of AI in overcoming the performance trade-offs inherent in traditional protein engineering. At the same time, it identifies existing challenges, such as data scarcity and insufficient model interpretability, and looks ahead to how multimodal gene-editing large language models and automated closed-loop experimental systems will drive the iterative development of miniaturized, broad-spectrum, and highly precise editing tools, thereby facilitating the clinical and industrial implementation of gene-editing technologies.

item.title: Autonomous Biogenesis of Early and Late Assembly Intermediates of a Large Ribosomal Subunit in a Minimal System.
item.abstract: Cell-free autonomous biogenesis of ribosomes is important for the bottom-up assembly of an artificial cell and for engineering of functional ribosomes with novel activities. The challenge lies in establishing conditions for a single-step multicomponent synthesis and assembly process in a minimal transcription-translation reaction. We previously reported autonomous synthesis and assembly of a bacterial small ribosomal subunit, but the assembly pathway of the large subunit is more complex with dozens of proteins that bind, fold, and chemically modify its ∼3000-base-long rRNA (rRNA). Here, we cosynthesized all the large subunit components including 33 ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) and 2 rRNAs from DNA brushes and followed the dynamics of assembly coupled to synthesis in real time using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy. A systematic screen of the binding of each of the ribosomal proteins to the 23S rRNA revealed an assembly pattern indicative of early intermediates. The addition of genes coding for six rRNA assembly factors facilitated binding of late assembly ribosomal proteins, supporting formation of late-stage intermediates even in the absence of rRNA modifications. We established a scenario for the large subunit biogenesis via macromolecular colocalization that may aid in the identification and characterization of additional genes required for achieving complete functional ribosome self-regeneration in a minimal system.

item.title: Synthetic genome shuffling of poxviruses in yeast generates novel poxvirus candidates with potential oncolytic properties.
item.abstract: Oncolytic viruses represent a promising class of biotherapeutics, yet their clinical performance is often constrained by limited cytolytic potency and insufficient immune activation. To address these limitations, we developed a synthetic biology framework that applies genome-scale recombination in yeast to generate chimeric poxviruses derived from multiple non-human-pathogenic poxvirus lineages. We first established the near-complete assembly of a vaccinia virus genome within yeast and demonstrated its ability to yield a functional virus in human cancer cells, providing a modular foundation for genome engineering. Building on this platform, we combined genomic inputs from different poxvirus species to create a diverse library of chimeric constructs, a subset of which could be recovered as infectious particles. Phenotypic characterization revealed substantial variation among chimeras, including distinct plaque morphologies, spreading behaviors, and activity across human cancer cell lines, indicating the emergence of functional diversity rather than incremental modification. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed that individual chimeras integrated genetic segments from several parental species, validating the broad recombination capacity of the yeast-based system. Collectively, these results establish a conceptual advance in synthetic virology. Yeast-mediated genome shuffling enables the rapid generation of functionally diverse chimeric poxviruses from multispecies inputs, providing a flexible and scalable platform for the identification and development of future oncolytic poxvirus candidates. While the chimeric viruses described here do not yet contain the attenuating mutations required for tumor-selective replication, they provide a foundation for the engineering of next-generation oncolytic biotherapeutics.

item.title: SmartPE enables efficient prime editing in dicot crops.
item.abstract: Prime editing (PE) in dicot plants is hindered by low efficiency and locus-dependent variability, limiting its broad application1. Here we present SmartPE, an optimized PE system that combines a dual-pegRNA strategy with designed mismatched bases in the reverse-transcription templates (RTTs), together with cis-regulatory elements and engineered reverse transcriptases. The editing efficiencies achieved with SmartPE in protoplasts of key dicot crops were substantially higher than those of canonical PE systems: 6.3-23.0-fold in Arabidopsis thaliana (Col-0), 8.2-38.2-fold in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), with over 10-fold improvements at the majority of target sites in soybean (Glycine max) and oilseed rape (Brassica napus). In tomato hairy roots, SmartPE generated homozygous (7.3%) and heterozygous (12.5%) edit lines at the SlOR2 locus, whereas standard PE produced only heterozygous edits (1.0%) and several chimeras. In stable transformation experiments, SmartPE enabled seamless insertion of a FLAG tag in Arabidopsis and insertion of enhancers and recombination sites in tomato, with editing efficiencies of up to 32.3%. Together, these results show that SmartPE provides an efficient PE framework for dicot species.

item.title: Beyond Cell Factory: In Vitro Biotransformation (ivBT): A Paradigm-Shifting Biomanufacturing Platform.
item.abstract: The paradigm of industrial biomanufacturing is shifting rapidly. Microbial fermentation mediated by cell factories is the dominant platform of biomanufacturing and has a history of thousands of years. However, their inherent properties, such as self-proliferation, cellular complexity, maintenance, and bioenergetic limits, could prevent them from being the best winner of biomanufacturing, especially for biocommodities and bioenergy. In this book chapter, we introduce a new concept of in vitro biotransformation (ivBT) as an emerging biomanufacturing platform that can surpass microbial cell factory. The development of ivBT is driven by the urgent great needs of food security and a new carbon-neutral energy society in the future. In theory, ivBT can have the theoretical yield and very high volumetric productivity and could have low-cost biomanufacturing costs. Furthermore, we highlight several representative applications, such as artificial photosynthesis for CO2-to-starch synthesis, in vitro respiration that can produce hydrogen under anaerobic conditions and electricity under aerobic conditions, directed glycosidic bond rearrangement (i.e., ATP-free or low-ATP biotransformation of cellulose to starch), and healthy sugars. Industrial biomanufacturing of myo-inositol, D-tagatose, and cellulosic starch would wipe off any prejudice (e.g., costly enzymes and short lifetime) and demonstrate transformative potential of ivBT. ivBT would be a paradigm-shifting biomanufacturing platform because it is like a dimensional reduction attack that can simplify extremely complicated cell factories by decreasing their dimensions.

item.title: Protocells with Fluorescent Response to Extracellular Signals.
item.abstract: This protocol describes the generation of protocells mimicking the signal transduction of living cells using giant unilamellar liposomes generated by the phase transfer method. This method allows the efficient encapsulation of cell-free protein synthesis reagents and plasmids encoding enzyme switches comprising an affinity tag, transmembrane domain, and β-glucuronidase mutant. Antibody binding to affinity tags on the protocell surface induces oligomerization and activation of the enzyme inside the protocells, producing a fluorescent signal from a fluorogenic substrate. The detailed procedure includes emulsion generation, liposome formation, protein synthesis inside the liposomes, and fluorescence detection. The protocells generated using this protocol provide a well-controlled system for studying signal transduction across membranes and the manipulation of physiological processes originating from living cells.

item.title: The Xenoreactome: Where Foreign Chemistry Becomes Biological Organization.
item.abstract: Biological systems can perform chemistry beyond their evolved reaction networks, but a reaction that is chemically possible does not necessarily occur in an intact system. I define the xenoreactome as the state- and reference-dependent network through which foreign chemistry enters a biological or cell-like system, is transformed and propagated, and is ultimately cleared or retained. The concept focuses on the factors that determine whether foreign chemistry is realized, including transport, localization, physiological state, downstream transfer, and clearance. Xenoreactomes may remain entirely molecular, carry non-native chemical or elemental features through existing biological machinery, or support reaction sequences with no direct biological counterpart, such as sustained free-radical vinyl polymerization. In some cases, xenochemical products can also accumulate sufficiently to form polymers, condensed phases, or other material states. For these systems, I introduce a simple quantitative criterion that relates xenochemical production and persistence to the threshold required for material formation. The xenoreactome provides a framework for asking which foreign chemistry biological systems can actually support, how far it propagates, and what ultimately happens to its products.

item.title: Artificial Cells and Biomimetic Cells: Intelligent Systems Driving a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery and Delivery.
item.abstract: The convergence of synthetic biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence drives a transformative shift in biopharmaceutical research, advancing from passive drug carriers to intelligent, programmable therapeutics. This review evaluates artificial and biomimetic cells as a framework that connects fundamental biological discovery with clinical translation. It examines five key technological pathways: membrane-engineered artificial cells, membraneless organelle (MLO) systems, multicompartmental artificial cells, protocell communication networks, and virtual cells. These platforms enable precise regulation of drug stability, targeting, biosynthesis, and adaptive responsiveness. Recent progress includes microenvironment-triggered release, logic-gated intercellular communication, and virtual cell-assisted high-throughput screening and toxicity prediction. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and regulatory adaptation. The integration of closed-loop learning, interpretable models, and advanced biomanufacturing will be essential to position artificial and biomimetic cell systems at the forefront of next-generation precision medicine.

item.title: Using the Function Prediction Server and Queryome for Functional Protein Design.
item.abstract: Accurate computational prediction of protein function is critical for guiding the functional design of proteins in the post-genomic era. The gap between the number of protein sequences deposited in databases and those with experimentally validated functional annotations continues to widen, making automated function prediction tools indispensable for researchers. In this chapter, we describe a suite of complementary computational tools for protein function prediction and literature-based functional analysis. We cover four sequence-based Gene Ontology (GO) term prediction methods available through the Protein Function Prediction web server: PFP, ESG (Extended Similarity Group), Phylo-PFP, and Domain-PFP. Each method leverages distinct algorithmic strategies, from mining distantly related sequences with PSI-BLAST to recursive multilevel sequence searches, phylogenetic distance-based reranking, and function-aware domain embeddings. We also describe Queryome, a multi-agent deep research system that performs evidence-grounded synthesis across 28.3 million PubMed abstracts, which can be used to contextualize and validate function predictions with primary literature evidence. We provide step-by-step protocols for using these tools, interpreting results, and integrating predictions into a workflow for the functional design of proteins. The Protein function prediction server is available at www.kiharalab.org/pfp and Queryome is available as a desktop application at www.queryome.app.

item.title: Natural and engineered bacteriophages against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: current landscape and clinical translation.
item.abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

item.title: Optogenetic Tool for Controlling p53 Signaling Pathway.
item.abstract: Optogenetics enables precise spatiotemporal control of intracellular processes by light and has become a powerful approach for manipulating cell signaling and gene expression. While chemical induction systems and synthetic biology-based tools such as Tet-regulated promoters and CRISPRa/CRISPRi provide versatile means to control gene expression, their temporal resolution and spatial specificity are limited by diffusion and degradation of chemical stimuli. Optogenetic strategies based on light-induced dimerization (LID) systems overcome these limitations and have enabled optical control of transcription factors and endogenous gene expression. However, most existing approaches focus on regulating individual genes or promoter elements, and methods to directly manipulate entire endogenous transcriptional networks in their physiological context remain limited. Here, we describe an optogenetic system, Opto-p53, which enables light-induced activation of endogenous p53 transcriptional activity by reconstituting its functional domains via a blue-light-inducible dimerization system. This protocol provides detailed procedures for cell line construction, light stimulation, imaging, and data analysis, offering a versatile platform to investigate p53-dependent transcriptional responses under controlled activation conditions.

item.title: Organoids and organs-on-a-chip as new approach methodologies at the convergence of cell biology and bioengineering.
item.abstract: The rapid growth of new approach methodologies (NAMs), including organoids and organs-on-a-chip (OOCs), has revealed a need for interdisciplinary dialogue between cell biologists and bioengineers to develop human models that can best complement therapeutic development. Stem cell-derived and bioengineered human tissue models are redefining how we understand human physiology and pathophysiology, offering control that traditional preclinical models cannot provide. By recapitulating complex tissue microenvironments, multi-organ interactions, and patient-specific biology, these systems are bridging long-standing gaps in the drug development and clinical application pipelines. Here, we synthesize advances in organoids, OOCs, and other bioengineered technologies for translational medicine to identify remaining gaps, including challenges in reproducibility, validation, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging opportunities at the intersection of synthetic biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and genetic engineering are positioning NAMs not merely as improved experimental tools but as foundational platforms for accelerating therapeutic discovery and enabling personalized medicine at scale.

item.title: Immune cell-derived exosomes in the tumor microenvironment: mechanisms of immune evasion and emerging therapeutic strategies in cancer immunotherapy.
item.abstract: Tumor-released exosomes have emerged from the shadows of "cellular dust" to be recognized as pivotal mediators of intercellular communication within the tumor microenvironment (TME). These nano-sized vesicles (30-150 nm) carry a complex cargo of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids that profoundly reshape anti-tumor immunity. This review comprehensively examines the dualistic nature of immune cell-derived exosomes in cancer progression, with particular focus on exosomes originating from B lymphoma cells, T lymphocytes, natural killer (NK) cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cell lineages including tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), mast cells, and neutrophils. We delineate the mechanistic pathways through which these exosomes disrupt the cancer immunity cycle suppressing CD8+ T cell activation via PD-L1/PD-1 engagement, inducing lymphocyte apoptosis through FasL and TRAIL, promoting regulatory T cell expansion, polarizing macrophages toward the M2 immunosuppressive phenotype, and establishing pre-metastatic niches through MMP-mediated extracellular matrix remodeling. The molecular machinery governing exosome biogenesis including ESCRT-dependent and ceramide-mediated pathways is critically reviewed, alongside the selective packaging mechanisms that concentrate immunosuppressive miRNAs (miR-155, miR-21, miR-23a, miR-223) into exosomal compartments. Importantly, we highlight the emerging therapeutic premises targeting these vesicles: pharmacological inhibition of exosome secretion (GW4869, Rab27a knockdown), checkpoint blockade reversing exosomal PD-L1-mediated T cell exhaustion, and the engineering of immunostimulatory exosomes as cell-free cancer vaccines establishing exosomes not merely as biomarkers of disease progression but as actionable therapeutic targets. The clinical translation of exosome-based diagnostics including liquid biopsy platforms detecting circulating tumor-derived exosomes and therapeutics that include engineered exosomes delivering immunomodulatory cargo represents a frontier in precision cancer immunotherapy.

item.title: Cellular origins and evolutionary dynamics of plasma cfDNA in solid tumors: integrating germline, tumor-derived, and hematopoietic variation for MRD and treatment guidance.
item.abstract: Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a heterogeneous and rapidly changing biological pool derived from malignant cells, normal tissues, and hematopoietic cells. The abundance and molecular composition of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) are determined not only by tumor burden but also by tissue architecture, vascular access, cell-death programs, chromatin organization, nuclease processing, systemic clearance, treatment exposure, and clonal evolution. These biological determinants shape the mutation, methylation, fragmentation, nucleosomal, and temporal features exploited by contemporary liquid-biopsy assays. Accurate clinical interpretation therefore requires both sensitive detection and reliable source attribution, particularly the distinction of tumor-derived variants from constitutional germline alterations and clonal hematopoiesis. In this review, we integrate the biological origins and processing of plasma cfDNA with analytical strategies for low-tumor-fraction detection and critically evaluate the evidence supporting postoperative molecular residual disease (MRD), recurrence surveillance, treatment-response assessment, resistance monitoring, and ctDNA-guided therapy across solid tumors. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing prognostic validity, treatment-predictive value, and demonstrated clinical utility. Current evidence is strongest in colorectal cancer and, more recently, ctDNA-selected urothelial cancer, whereas routine ctDNA-directed intervention in resected non-small cell lung cancer and breast cancer remains insufficiently validated. By linking cfDNA biology to an explicit hierarchy of clinical evidence, this review defines both the established applications and the major limitations that must be addressed before broader implementation of ctDNA-guided precision oncology.
